title: Increasing Order Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting values and building a new chain versus rewiring existing nodes in place during in-order traversal.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree, rearrange the tree in in-order so that the resulting tree has no left children, every node has only a right child, forming a single increasing chain.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root, a BST"],["Output","The same nodes rearranged into a right-leaning chain in sorted order"],["Goal","Rewire nodes in place during an in-order traversal, without creating new nodes"],["Constraints","Up to 100 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: Since in-order traversal already visits BST nodes in sorted order, rewiring each node's left pointer to null and its right pointer to the NEXT node visited (during the same traversal) directly produces the required right-leaning chain, without needing to build any new nodes.

blocks.title: Analogy: Restringing Beads Already in Sorted Order onto a Single Thread
blocks.text: Picture beads already organized in a tree-like display, but sorted correctly if read in a particular traversal order. Restringing them onto a single straight thread, in that same traversal order, produces the desired single chain, reusing the same beads rather than making new ones.

blocks.caption: During in-order traversal, rewire each node's left to null and right to the next node visited

blocks.text: Result (preorder, now a straight chain): 1 null 2 null 3 null 4 null 5 null 6 null 7 null 8 null 9 null null.

Before building a fresh chain of new nodes from collected sorted values, notice that in-order traversal already visits nodes in the correct final order, so REUSING each node and just rewiring its pointers during the traversal directly produces the answer in place.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits nodes in strictly increasing order, exactly the order needed for the final chain.

Observation 2: Maintaining a "current tail" pointer to the last node placed into the chain, each newly visited node can be attached as that tail's right child, then become the new tail.

Observation 3: Each visited node's own left pointer must be cleared (set to null), since the final structure has no left children anywhere.

Observation 4: Using a dummy placeholder node before starting simplifies attaching the very first visited node, avoiding a special case.
This leads to an in-order traversal that, for each visited node, clears its left pointer and attaches it as the right child of a running "tail" pointer, updating the tail to this node.
Collect all node values via in-order traversal, then build a brand new chain of fresh nodes from this sorted list.
Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting values then building fresh nodes directly produces the correct sorted chain.
It allocates n new nodes unnecessarily, when the existing nodes could simply be rewired.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the values list, plus n new node allocations.
Limitation: rewiring existing nodes DURING the in-order traversal avoids ever needing a separate values list or new node allocations.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since in-order traversal visits nodes in the exact order needed, rewiring each visited node's pointers in place (left to null, right to the next visited node) during the SAME traversal directly builds the final structure, with no separate collection step and no new node allocations.
In-order traversal with a running tail pointer (starting at a dummy node): for each visited node, clear its left pointer, attach it as the tail's right child, and update the tail to this node.

codes.python:
def increasing_bst(root):
    dummy = TreeNode(0)
    cur = [dummy]
    def inorder(node):
        if not node:
            return
        inorder(node.left)
        node.left = None                      # clear left pointer
        cur[0].right = node                     # attach as tail's right child
        cur[0] = node                            # update tail
        inorder(node.right)
    inorder(root)
    return dummy.right

blocks.text: Since in-order traversal visits BST nodes in exactly the order the final chain needs, rewiring each node's pointers as it is visited (rather than afterward) builds the correct structure directly, reusing all original nodes without any extra allocation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(height) recursion depth, O(1) extra beyond that (no new nodes).
